Pressure Control: Weighting, Unweighting and Pumping

Performance outcome

The rider adds and removes pressure through the bike on purpose: pushing into the back sides of rollers, compressions and downslopes to gain speed, and going light over obstacles to keep it, so they can carry speed without pedalling.

Who it’s for

Advanced riders who can ride a pump track or flowing trail and want to turn terrain into speed; downhill and enduro racers working on sections where pedalling isn’t possible.

Before this lesson

  • Solid bike/body separation (see Advanced Body Position).
  • Can ride a pump track or rolling trail continuously in control.

Why it matters

Speed you don’t lose is speed you don’t need to make up. On many race sections there is no room to pedal, and pressure control is how fast riders make time anyway.

Technical model

Weighting and unweighting

Pressing down through the feet and hands increases the force between tyres and ground; pulling the body up and letting the bike come up reduces it. Smooth surfaces and pump tracks are the place to learn the rhythm before applying it on trail.

Where pushing helps and where it hurts

Pushing the bike down into a downslope (the back side of a roller, rock or ledge) turns the slope into forward speed. Pushing into an upslope does the opposite. Pumping means timing pressure to the shape of the ground.

Going light over obstacles

Before roots or rocks, compressing into the ground and then going light, much like the start of a bunny hop, lets the bike skim over instead of crashing into them. Weight settles back onto the bike on smoother ground.

Coasting can beat pedalling

In tight gaps, off-camber sections and rough ground, pedalling risks pedal strikes and puts the body in a poor position to absorb. Coasting and pumping can be faster.

Linked corners

Between linked corners, pedalling disrupts weight and line into the second one. Staying light out of the first and loading the bike through the second, while picking the line, often carries more speed. A single well-timed pedal stroke as the bike comes upright can then carry speed out of a corner.

Physics & maths

How pumping adds energy

Pumping is the same physics as pumping a playground swing: the rider does work by extending and compressing at the right moments. Pushing down as the bike goes down the back of a roller adds to the forward force from the slope, so kinetic energy increases; going light up the front reduces the energy lost climbing it. Mathematically, the rider is doing work against the normal force, and the timing of that work relative to the slope decides whether it speeds them up or slows them down.

A good Mathlete visual: a roller profile with the force arrows, showing why the same push helps on the back side and hurts on the front.

Common errors

What you seePossible causesCorrection
Pushing into the front (up) side of rollers.Timing too early; not looking far enough ahead to see the shape; too much speed for the spacing.Coach to supply
Pedalling in rough or tight sections and losing speed.Habit; not trusting that coasting is faster; pedal strikes.Coach to supply
Arms do all the pumping; legs stay stiff.Position too far forward; not enough leg range.Coach to supply
Pumping looks big but speed doesn’t increase.Movement is up-and-down rather than timed to the slope; effort without timing.Coach to supply

Practice design

Setting
A pump track or a smooth rolling section, then a familiar trail section with clear downslopes. Coach-selected and low consequence.
Focus
One feature at a time: for example, gain speed from a single back side without pedalling.
Feedback
Compare exit speed or a short timed segment over several runs with no pedalling allowed; film from the side.

Stop when

  • Fatigue (pumping is tiring and timing degrades quickly).
  • The rider starts adding speed rather than refining timing.

Video analysis

What the rider and coach look for in footage:

  • Timing: is pressure added on the back sides and removed on the faces?
  • Leg and arm use: do both contribute?
  • Speed carried through the section without pedalling.
  • Smoothness of the hips’ path.
  • Consistency over several runs.

Ready to move on

  • Coach-observed: the rider gains speed through a rhythm section without pedalling, consistently.
  • The rider can pick out, on a trail they know, where pumping helps and where pedalling is worth it.

Educational checkpoints, not safety certificates.

Safety

Class 2: advanced riding skills. Needs the stated prerequisites, a controlled progression, suitable terrain and coaching guidance.

Practice only on terrain your coach has chosen, within your current skill, with the right protective equipment. Completing a lesson isn’t a safety certificate and doesn’t mean a rider is ready to try anything.
